deviations.summary: A recorded allergy has no date — frame 42 shows one ('2019')
deviations.reason: Frame 42 dates the permanent medical fact: 'Penicillin allergy recorded — 2019'. The patient record stores allergies as encrypted free text with no timestamp and no author, so there is no year to show. The entry carries a null date and is pinned under 'ON RECORD' at the end of the timeline rather than being given a fabricated one — a wrong date on a clinical fact is worse than no date, because it invites reasoning about when the patient developed it.
deviations.openQuestion: Should allergies become dated, authored records rather than a free-text column? That is a clinical data-model decision — it would let the timeline show when and by whom — and it needs your ruling before any schema change.

deviations.summary: The seed recorded the same allergy in one place and not the other
deviations.reason: Akhilesh carried medicalFlags ['PENICILLIN_ALLERGY'] but no allergiesEnc. The in-chair card reads flags and the history reads the encrypted field, so the demo asserted the patient was allergic on one screen and silent about it on another. Both now carry it.
deviations.fixedIn: packages/db/prisma/seed.ts sets medicalFlags and allergiesEnc together.

deviations.summary: Re-running the seed failed on the lab case's unique caseNumber
deviations.reason: The new lab-case fixture cleaned up by treatmentPlanId, but the plan is recreated with a fresh id on every run, so the delete never matched the previous run's case and the second seed died on (clinicId, caseNumber). `pnpm db:seed` is the documented way back to a known demo; it has to survive being run twice.
deviations.fixedIn: Deletes by caseNumber. Verified by running the seed twice in a row.

deviations.summary: The visit-record sheet needs FINDINGS and PROCEDURE prose that is not extracted
deviations.reason:
Frame 43 is a read-only record of one visit, and its body is two narrative sections — FINDINGS ('Deep caries distal 36, tenderness on percussion...') and PROCEDURE ('Access opening under LA, four canals located...'). ClinicalExtraction has one free-text field, `notes`, which is where dictated patient advice lands; there is no findings field and no procedure narrative. The rest of the sheet is buildable — audioDurationMs exists, bills and prescriptions are joinable, and Amend has its append-only ConsultationEdit path — but a visit record whose two clinical sections are empty is not the record the frame describes, and generating that prose is exactly what product rule 7 forbids.

Sitting rows on frame 39 therefore do not offer to open it: they render without a chevron rather than as buttons that lead somewhere disappointing.
deviations.openQuestion: Same dependency as #52 — add `findings` and `procedureNarrative` to ClinicalExtraction and the clinical prompt. Recommend scheduling both with extraction work, where the prompt and its tests live, rather than inside a UI task.
deviations.ownerRuling: 2026-09-07 - OWNER RULING, verbatim: 'Build the fixture, defer the fields.' `findings` and `procedureNarrative` are NOT added to ClinicalExtraction and the clinical prompt is NOT changed as part of this UI migration - changing what the AI extracts has its own blast radius and needs its own clinical review. PaperBlock and the visit record render the sections that HAVE data and omit the sections that do not; they never generate prose to fill them (product rule 7). These frames are recorded rather than force-matched.

deviations.summary: CLINICAL: frame 45 LOCKS 'Share Rx PDF' while an allergy conflict is unresolved
deviations.reason:
Frame 45 greys the share button and captions it 'Locked while a conflict is unresolved'. That is a clinical hard block, and product rules 4 and 8 reserve those for you: the dentist is the final clinical decision maker, and a hard-block policy must come from an explicit clinical decision rather than from matching a frame.

You already ruled the equivalent question on the verification card (#53): Confirm stays available over an allergy conflict, the dentist may override, and the override is audited. The consistent answer here is that Share stays available.

But it is NOT obviously the same act, which is why I am not deciding it. Confirming a record files what happened. Sharing a prescription PDF hands the patient a document telling them to take a drug the record says they react to — the artefact leaves the clinic and outlives the conversation. A hard block is more defensible here than on Confirm.

NOT IMPLEMENTED. Share remains available and the conflict is drawn loudly on the drug itself.
deviations.openQuestion: Three options. (a) Consistent with #53: Share stays available, conflict shown loudly, override audited. (b) Hard block per the frame. (c) Middle: Share stays available but requires an explicit acknowledgement that is recorded, the way confirmedWithWarning already works. I recommend (c) — it keeps the dentist deciding while making the decision auditable on a document that leaves the building. Either (b) or (c) is a clinical-policy decision and needs your ruling.
deviations.ownerRuling: 2026-09-07 - OWNER RULING, verbatim: 'Share stays available, log it.' Share Rx PDF is NOT locked by an unresolved allergy conflict. This is consistent with ruling #53 on the verification card: an allergy warning is advisory, the dentist is the final clinical decision maker, and the override is audited. Sharing over an unresolved conflict is recorded as a share-with-warning audit event. Frame 45's greyed button and its 'Locked while a conflict is unresolved' caption are therefore NOT implemented; the conflict rail still renders prominently above the share control.
deviations.resolution: Share control stays enabled. The conflict rail renders above it. Taking Share while a conflict is open emits an audited share-with-warning event, mirroring CONSULTATION_CONFIRMED_WITH_WARNING.

deviations.summary: Frame 45's 'Swap' chip is an automatic drug substitution — forbidden by rule 6
deviations.reason: The conflict row in frame 45 offers a pine 'Swap' chip beside 'Remove'. Swapping means naming a replacement drug, which product rule 6 forbids outright ('AI must not invent medication substitutions') and which #51 already records as having no knowledge base behind it. The row ships with 'Remove', which is the action the safety model actually recognises as resolving the conflict, and it says Remove so the doctor is never told the app chose a replacement.
deviations.openQuestion: Same dependency as #51 — a substitution knowledge base with clinical sign-off.

deviations.summary: Conflicts are shown only where the SERVER flagged them, never computed on the client
deviations.reason: Frame 45 marks the offending medicine. The implementation renders exactly the warnings the safety layer returned, keyed to the drug they name. It does NOT match medicine names against the patient's allergies itself: doing so would mean asserting that amoxicillin is a penicillin — clinical class knowledge the app does not have (#51) — and product rule 7 forbids converting that uncertainty into clinical truth. A medicine typed by hand therefore carries no flag unless the server flagged it, which is honest about what the app actually knows.
deviations.ruling: Self-resolved: rules 6 and 7 already decide it; nothing new is being chosen.

deviations.summary: GOVERNANCE: standing authority to rule non-clinical product decisions, with a reversible log
deviations.reason:
2026-09-07 - OWNER RULING, verbatim: 'Decide non-clinical, log it.' Layout, copy, workflow and information-architecture decisions are the agent's to make during this migration rather than stalling it. Each such decision is recorded here as an APPROVED-DEVIATION carrying its reasoning, and the owner receives one review list at the end which they may reverse in whole or in part.

UNCHANGED AND STILL BLOCKING: clinical decisions, privacy/RBAC decisions, anything touching PHI, removal of existing functionality, and clinical hard-block policy. Those classify the frame BLOCKED and wait for the owner, exactly as before. Product rules 1-8 in CLAUDE.md are not re-litigable under this authority.
deviations.ownerRuling: Decide non-clinical, log it. Clinical, privacy/RBAC and PHI still block and wait.

deviations.summary: GATE C: a frame does not close until its screen actually works
deviations.reason: 2026-09-07 - OWNER DIRECTION, verbatim: 'in the end i want complete end to end working app.' Visual fidelity is necessary but not sufficient. On top of Gate A (nothing lost) and Gate B (matches the design), every frame must pass Gate C: the route is reachable through real navigation; every control on it is wired to a real endpoint or a real client action; the flow it belongs to can be completed end to end against the live API with seeded data; and there are no dead buttons, placeholder screens or TODO surfaces. A screen that photographs correctly but does nothing is NOT complete.

deviations.summary: The conflict line states the allergy and the class; it cannot state when it was recorded or the reaction
deviations.reason:
Frame 27's line reads 'Penicillin allergy — recorded 2019, reaction: rash'. The record stores an allergy as encrypted free text (Patient.allergiesEnc) plus a medicalFlags enum. There is no recorded-on date and no reaction field, so two thirds of that line has nothing behind it. Inventing them is exactly what product rule 7 forbids — turning uncertain information into clinical truth on screen.

So the line says what is actually known and why it matters: 'Allergy conflict: patient lists Penicillin. Amoxicillin is a penicillin. Verify before prescribing.' It is longer than the frame's and wraps to three lines rather than two. That cost is accepted: the frame's compactness comes from data the clinic never captured.

If the allergy model later gains a recorded-at and a reaction, this line should shorten to the frame's shape.

deviations.summary: The resolved warning lands in the SAFETY banner, not inline on a swapped row
deviations.reason:
Frame 28 shows the resolution on the row itself: 'Azithromycin 500 — swapped for Amoxicillin · allergy-safe [Undo]'. That shape depends on deviation #51 — a swap the app deliberately does not perform, because product rule 6 forbids the AI inventing a medication substitution.

Resolving by REMOVAL leaves no row for the resolved warning to sit on. Dropping it there would break the card's stated invariant that a resolved warning re-renders with a check and is never silently removed — 'I dealt with that' must not look like 'nothing was ever raised'. So partitionSafety() routes it to the standalone SAFETY block, struck through with a check.

The consequence visible in the capture: medicine count reads 'Medicines · 1' where the frame reads 2, because the conflicting drug is gone rather than replaced.

deviations.summary: NEXT SITTING shows the date; the frame also shows a time and the procedure
deviations.reason:
The frame reads 'Thu 16 Jul · 10:00 · obturation'. What the extraction produces is a follow-up INTERVAL ('review next week') — afterDays — not a booked slot. There is no time because nothing has been scheduled yet, and no procedure name because the next sitting's procedure is not dictated.

Printing a plausible 10:00 would be a fabricated appointment a receptionist could act on. The tile shows the date it can derive and stays a link to the real booking flow, where a time is chosen against actual availability.

deviations.summary: The card keeps an '+ Add medicine' affordance and a procedure sub-label the frames do not draw
deviations.reason:
Two additions the frames do not show, both retained under the Gate A rule that functionality is never removed for pixel fidelity:

1. '+ Add medicine' — the doctor must be able to add a drug the dictation missed. Without it the only route is re-recording the whole consultation.
2. The TOOTH tile carries the procedure ('RCT') beneath the number. The frame's tile shows the number alone; the tooth and what was done to it are read together everywhere else in this app.

Both are additive and neither displaces frame content.

deviations.summary: The prose region is empty, leaving vertical space the frames fill with FINDINGS and PROCEDURE
deviations.reason:
A visible consequence of ruling #52/#90 rather than a separate decision, recorded because it is what a reviewer sees first in the side-by-side: with no findings or procedure narrative extracted, the band between the medicine list and the CTA is blank, where the frames carry two paragraphs.

The sections are omitted rather than filled — PaperBlock renders what has data and never generates prose (product rule 7). The layout is not re-tuned to close the gap, because the gap is honest: it shows the record is thinner than the design assumed, and it will fill in on its own if the extraction fields are added later.

deviations.summary: GATE C FIX: the medicine row was a <button> containing the Remove and Undo buttons
deviations.reason:
Found while driving frame 28's capture. MedicineRow wrapped its whole body in a <button> whenever it had an onClick, so the conflict's 'Remove' chip and the resolved row's 'Undo' were buttons nested inside a button. React logged it on every render ('In HTML, %s cannot be a descendant of <%s>').

It was not only invalid. A button's accessible name is the concatenation of its contents, so the row announced itself as 'Amoxicillin 500mg TID 5 days Allergy conflict: patient lists Penicillin … Remove'. A screen-reader user could not distinguish the row from the action inside it — and the capture driver could not either: getByRole('button', { name: /remove/i }) matched the ROW and clicked that instead, which is how it surfaced.

The row is now a div with a stretched hit-area button behind content that ignores pointer events; the real actions opt back in above it. Pixel-identical, correctly nested, and the row carries an explicit name of its own.

deviations.summary: A voiced allergy lands inside 'More details' instead of a prominent chip
deviations.reason:
Frame 36 puts the allergy in the flags row as a red 'Allergy: Penicillin' chip, beside Diabetes/BP/Thyroid — visible without scrolling or expanding anything.

The implementation captures it correctly: extractPatientIntake parses 'allergic to penicillin', the form writes it to the ALLERGIES field, and setMoreOpen(true) auto-expands the section so it is not silently hidden. But that section sits below the fold, so the most safety-critical fact the intake captured is the least visible thing on the screen, while six medical-flag chips the patient does NOT have occupy the prominent row.

This is a MUST-FIX rather than a deviation because the frame and product rule 2 agree: doctor-facing clinical surfaces must surface allergies prominently, and /patients/new is doctor-only. Implementing the frame here IS implementing the rule; no product decision is needed.

Fix: render voiced allergies as crit-toned chips in the FLAGS row, keeping the free-text ALLERGIES field in More details as the editable source of truth. Owned by Task 20.
deviations.resolution: Fixed 2026-09-08: voiced allergies render as crit chips in the form body, above FLAGS. The free-text ALLERGIES field under More details stays the editable source of truth; the chip is a readout, so the two cannot drift.

deviations.summary: CHIEF COMPLAINT is a primary field in the frame and an expandable one in the app
deviations.reason:
Frame 36 shows CHIEF COMPLAINT as a first-class field between AGE & GENDER and MEDICAL FLAGS, filled and wearing the lime voice spine ('Pain on chewing, lower left'). The implementation puts it inside 'More details' alongside address and blood group.

The chief complaint is why the patient is here. It is the field the doctor reads first and the one the dictation is most likely to fill; grouping it with 'referred by' misreads its weight. Same root as #102 — the form's primary/secondary split does not match the frame's, and the frame's is right.

Owned by Task 20, which owns frames 35 and 36.
deviations.resolution: Fixed 2026-09-08: CHIEF COMPLAINT is a primary field between AGE/GENDER and the flags, as the frame has it.

deviations.summary: The patient code is generated and shown in the title, not as a short 'P-0413' chip
deviations.reason:
The frame shows a tidy 'P-0413' chip top-right and repeats it in the CTA ('Create patient · P-0413'). The app generates codes with a collision-resistant scheme and shows the real one — 'PT-PDFUHW' in this capture — in the header.

The frame's format implies a per-clinic sequential counter. That is a schema and concurrency decision (two receptionists creating patients at once must not both get P-0413), not a visual one, and the existing generator already solves it. Showing a prettier code than the record actually carries would mean the chip and the database disagree.

Recorded rather than matched. If sequential per-clinic codes are wanted, that is its own task with its own uniqueness story.

deviations.summary: The dictation card carries a full-width CTA where the frame has a mic circle
deviations.reason:
The frame's 'Say the details' card ends in a compact lime mic circle. The implementation renders a full-width 'Speak patient details' pill beneath the example line.

A bare mic circle reads as decoration next to an example sentence in quotes; in testing the labelled control is what makes it obvious the app is waiting to be spoken to, which is the whole premise of the product. The card is taller as a result and pushes the form down by roughly one field.

Kept deliberately. Decided under #94 as an interface decision, and reversible if the owner prefers the frame's restraint.

deviations.summary: AGE and GENDER keep their own labels where the frame uses one 'AGE & GENDER'
deviations.reason:
The frame labels the shared row once, 'AGE & GENDER'. The implementation keeps a label per field on the same row.

They are two separate inputs with separate validation and separate error slots — age can be invalid while gender is fine, and an error under a joint label cannot say which half it belongs to. The row grouping, which is what the frame is really doing, is matched.

deviations.summary: FLAGS is a full picker; the frame shows only the flags that are set plus a '+'
deviations.reason:
Frame 36 shows three chips — Diabetes, BP, Thyroid — and a '+' to add more. That is a SUMMARY of what is set on an existing record.

This screen is the opposite situation: a form being filled for the first time, where the receptionist has to find the right flag rather than review chosen ones. Showing all six as a multi-select makes the vocabulary discoverable; a '+' hides it behind a tap and a second surface. Voice-extracted flags outside the standard six still render as pre-selected custom chips, so nothing dictated is lost either way.

The frame's treatment is the better one on a record being reviewed, and the patient-detail surfaces use it there.

deviations.summary: A doctor's More hub shows three module tiles; the frame draws four, including Billing
deviations.reason:
Frame 70 shows Lab, Messages, Inventory and Billing. The capture is a DOCTOR session and shows three: `/billing` is RECEPTIONIST/ADMIN in lib/rbac.ts, so `canAccess('/billing', role)` hides the tile.

This is the rule working, not a missing tile. Rendering a route the role cannot open leaks the shape of the permission model and hands the user a tile that 403s. The frame depicts a reception or admin view, where all four appear.

The module grid reflows from four tiles to three; nothing else moves.

deviations.summary: Hub values are absent rather than zero while their query is loading or failed
deviations.reason:
Every chip on this hub — '1 doctor', '2 upcoming', '12', '1 request' — renders only when its query has answered with a non-zero value. A loading or failed query renders no chip at all.

The alternative is a chip that reads '0 doctors' for a moment and then corrects itself. A clinic always has at least one doctor, so zero is never a fact about the clinic; it is only ever a fact about the request, and printing it tells the reader something false about their own clinic.

So the frame's populated hub is what a loaded hub looks like, and an unloaded one is quieter than the frame rather than wrong.

deviations.summary: DoctorAvailability's unique constraint never fires — nullable effectiveFrom makes every always-row distinct
deviations.reason:
`@@unique([doctorId, dayOfWeek, startTime, effectiveFrom])` looks like it prevents duplicate windows. It does not. `effectiveFrom` is nullable and means "always"; every row in the dev database has it null. Postgres treats NULLs as DISTINCT in a unique index, so two identical always-rows are not duplicates and the constraint has never applied to a single row.

Two consequences, one already seen:

1. The seed used createMany({ skipDuplicates: true }) and believed itself idempotent. skipDuplicates only skips what the index calls a duplicate, so every run appended six more windows. The dev clinic reached 27 identical windows per weekday and the availability screen rendered as an unreadable wall of chips — which is how this was found.
2. The APPLICATION has the same hole: POST /doctors/:id/availability calls create() with no guard, so a receptionist who taps Add twice gets two identical windows, and the booking engine then reads a doctor as doubly available.

The seed is fixed by upserting on a deterministic id (verified: two consecutive runs leave six rows). That works around it for seeded data only. The constraint itself still needs correcting so the application cannot create duplicates either.

Postgres is 16, so the index can express this directly:

  DELETE FROM "DoctorAvailability" a USING "DoctorAvailability" b
   WHERE a."doctorId" = b."doctorId" AND a."dayOfWeek" = b."dayOfWeek"
     AND a."startTime" = b."startTime"
     AND a."effectiveFrom" IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b."effectiveFrom"
     AND a.ctid > b.ctid;
  DROP INDEX "DoctorAvailability_doctorId_dayOfWeek_startTime_effectiveFrom_key";
  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "DoctorAvailability_doctorId_dayOfWeek_startTime_effectiveFrom_key"
    ON "DoctorAvailability" ("doctorId", "dayOfWeek", "startTime", "effectiveFrom") NULLS NOT DISTINCT;

Prisma cannot express NULLS NOT DISTINCT in schema.prisma, so this wants a hand-written migration plus a note on the model, and it deserves its own task rather than riding along inside a UI migration. Worth auditing the other nullable columns that appear in @@unique lists for the same flaw.
deviations.resolution: Fixed 2026-09-09 by migration 20260909090000_availability_unique_nulls_not_distinct: existing duplicates collapsed, then the unique index rebuilt with NULLS NOT DISTINCT so two identical always-rows finally count as duplicates. Verified against the live database — an INSERT of an existing (doctorId, dayOfWeek, startTime, null) row is now rejected. POST /availability/doctor/:id answers the violation with 409 AVAILABILITY_DUPLICATE rather than a 500, and four tests cover it, including that a second window at a DIFFERENT time on the same day is still allowed — the frame's own morning/afternoon split depends on that. schema.prisma carries a warning that regenerating the index from schema alone silently drops the NULLS NOT DISTINCT clause.

deviations.summary: The doctor switcher appears only when there is more than one doctor
deviations.reason:
Frame 73 shows a two-tab switcher, Dr. Priya / Dr. Arjun. The seeded clinic has one dentist, so the implementation renders her name as a heading instead: a lone selected tab is a control that cannot be operated, and it invites the reader to look for the other one.

The switcher is built and renders as the frame draws it as soon as a clinic has a second doctor.

The hours themselves also differ from the frame — one 09:00–18:00 window per weekday against the frame's split 09:30–13:00 / 14:00–20:30 and its short Saturday. That is seed data, not design: the row renders however many windows a day has.

deviations.summary: The booking-conflict note says what the app does, which is less than the frame promises
deviations.reason:
Frame 74's note reads: 'A date with existing bookings can't be blocked — Odovox shows the count and offers to move them first.'

The first half is true and enforced: POST /day-off rejects a date carrying appointments with DAY_OFF_HAS_APPOINTMENTS and the count, which the page surfaces as 'N appointments already booked — move them first'. The second half is not: there is no affordance that moves them. Offering one would need a bulk-reschedule flow that does not exist.

So the note says 'Odovox names the count so those appointments get moved first'. Copy that promises a button the screen does not have is worse than copy that is shorter than the frame's, particularly on a screen whose whole job is to stop someone closing a day out from under a booked patient.

If the bulk-reschedule flow is built, this copy should return to the frame's wording.

deviations.summary: The scope selector names the doctors instead of offering a generic 'A doctor'
deviations.reason:
The implementation previously offered 'Whole clinic | A doctor', where choosing the second revealed a dropdown to then pick the person — a category step in front of a choice that is already just a short list of names.

It now lists 'Whole clinic' plus one tab per doctor, which is what frame 74 draws (Whole clinic / Dr. Priya / Dr. Arjun) and one decision rather than two. The row scrolls horizontally for a clinic with several dentists.

deviations.summary: The switches name intents; the API's Meta template keys are grouped behind them
deviations.reason:
Frame 72's 'Automatic messages' has four switches with human names. The implementation had six rows carrying raw template keys — `appointment_reminder_1h`, `outstanding_balance_reminder` — which are Meta's identifiers, not decisions a dentist makes. Deciding whether to chase patients for money should not require knowing the chase is called `outstanding_balance_reminder`, or that 'remind them about the appointment' is two approved templates that both have to be on.

Grouping is by key prefix (lib/whatsapp/template-groups.ts, 14 tests) so a newly approved template lands in the right group without a code change. A group is ON when any member is on, and one tap sets them all — which is what a single switch above several templates already appeared to promise.

One difference from the frame's set: it shows 'Review requests' and this clinic has no such approved template, while it does have `prescription_ready`, which the frame lacks. The groups follow the templates that exist. Anything unrecognised keeps its own row rather than vanishing — a message going to patients that nobody can see on this screen is the failure worth avoiding.

deviations.summary: PRIVACY: the business number is masked and the provider name is gone
deviations.reason:
The card printed the full WhatsApp Business number and a 'Provider: mock' line. Frame 72 masks the number ('+91 98··· ··00') and shows no provider, and it is right on both.

The card's question is 'are we connected', not 'what is the number'. This screen is readable by any clinic role and is routinely on display when someone is being shown around, and the number identifies the clinic's messaging account. It now reads 'Business · +91 80····0000'.

The provider is a deployment detail that tells a dentist nothing and actively misleads when it reads 'mock' — which looks like a fault on a screen whose whole job is to say the integration is healthy.

deviations.summary: Monthly spend shows ₹0 against the frame's ₹620 of ₹1,000, and the cap footnote is omitted
deviations.reason:
Two content differences on the spend section.

The numbers are seed data: no conversations have been billed, so the total is ₹0 and the six-month chart is empty. The chart now states that in words rather than drawing bars — and it renders a fixed six-month axis regardless, because plotting only the months that exist gave a first-month clinic ONE bar stretched across the full width, a single data point drawn as though it were a trend (lastSixMonths, 4 tests).

The frame's footnote — 'At the cap, sends pause and a banner appears on Today' — is NOT reproduced. A budget cap and a warning threshold exist, but whether reaching the cap actually halts sending and raises a banner on Today is not something this screen can assert from what is implemented, and copy describing a safety behaviour that may not happen is worse than no copy on a screen about spending real money. It should return once that path is verified end to end.

deviations.summary: Archive moved from a per-row icon into the template editor
deviations.reason:
The list carried a pencil and an archive icon beside every template. Frame 75 has neither — a name, its chips and a chevron — because this screen is a PICKER before it is a manager: the question is 'which bundle', and four templates used to fill the whole screen.

Rebuilt to the frame, tapping a row opens the editor, which is what the chevron implies. Archive follows it there rather than being removed: it sits below Save as a quiet text action. Archiving is rare and feels destructive, and an icon permanently beside every name invited a mis-tap on the screen people use most often to just choose one.

Gate A holds — nothing was removed, it moved one tap deeper, behind the same permission check (`canManage && mine`) the icons had.

deviations.summary: Chips read the clinic's own tags where the frame shows a curated set
deviations.reason:
The frame's rows carry '3 meds' plus a category ('RCT', 'Pedo · wt-based') and an age band ('Adult'). The implementation shows the medicine count plus the template's first two actual tags — 'antibiotic', 'post-op', 'periodontal'.

Tags are free text the clinic writes, so there is no category or age-band field to render, and inventing one would mean classifying a dentist's own templates on their behalf. Two tags, because a third pushed the row to wrap and the frame's whole point here is a list that scans in one pass.

The footnote is also shortened: the frame cites the prescription sheet by frame number ('the prescription sheet (23)'), which is spec shorthand, not something to show a user.

deviations.summary: Add stays a floating FAB where the frame puts a + in the header
deviations.reason:
Frame 67 draws a lime + at the top right. The implementation keeps the FabMenu at the bottom right, which is this app's convention everywhere else — and frame 57 draws the lab's + as its own bottom dial, so the frames are not consistent with each other on this point either.

Moving it on this one screen would make inventory the odd surface. The cost is that the FAB floats over the last visible row until you scroll, which the frame's placement avoids; that is the trade being made deliberately rather than by omission.

What DID change is what the + holds. The three voice actions were its first three entries — two taps from the screen — while New item and New category sat below them. On a product whose thesis is that the dentist speaks instead of typing, that is backwards. The voice actions are now chips under the title, as the frame has them, and the FAB keeps the typed paths.

deviations.summary: 'Reorder all' has no supplier-ordering concept behind it
deviations.reason:
The frame puts 'Reorder all' beside the Low stock heading. There is nothing for it to do: `reorderLevel` is a THRESHOLD that marks an item low, and the only related endpoint is POST /inventory/items/:id/purchase, which RECORDS stock arriving. Nothing in the schema represents a purchase order, a supplier, or an outbound request.

So the control is omitted rather than wired to something that resembles it. Gate C forbids a button that does nothing, and 'Reorder all' silently recording a purchase that never happened would be worse than absent — it would inflate stock counts for items the clinic has not received.

Building it means deciding what reordering IS for this product: an internal shopping list, a WhatsApp message to a supplier, or a tracked purchase order. That is a product decision, and it belongs to whoever owns supplier workflow rather than to a visual migration.

deviations.summary: Rows keep their stock-tone spine and the screen keeps search and category filters
deviations.reason:
The frame's item rows sit flat inside one card. The implementation's rows are separate cards carrying a coloured left spine — crit when below the reorder level, warn when expiring, sage otherwise — so the state of the stock is legible without reading the number. The frame conveys the same thing with a peach badge on low-stock rows only; the spine also covers expiry, which the frame shows as a separate crit chip.

The screen also keeps a search field and category filter chips the frame does not draw. A seeded clinic has 7 items and the frame's has 64; at 64 the list is not scannable without them, and removing working filters for pixel fidelity is exactly what Gate A forbids.

deviations.summary: The second tile falls back to the category when an item has no price, vendor or expiry
deviations.reason:
Frame 68's right-hand tile reads '₹ / STRIP · VENDOR · ₹42 · MedPlus · Exp Mar 2027'. That is an item with a purchase history. A composite resin nobody has recorded a purchase for has none of those three facts, and rendering the tile with '—' in it restates the emptiness in a bigger font than the old list did.

So the tile shows whichever of price, vendor and expiry exist, and when none do it shows the category instead — a fact every item has, and the one the row above it was already carrying. The tile is never empty and never lies.

The replaced DETAILS list rendered five key/value rows regardless, most of them '—' on a real item, which made an ordinary item look unrecorded rather than uncomplicated.

deviations.summary: SKU and batch survive the removed DETAILS list as one conditional line
deviations.reason:
Frame 68 shows neither. The DETAILS list this replaced showed both, so dropping the list wholesale would have taken them with it — for an item that actually HAS a SKU that is losing a fact, not tidying one away, and Gate A does not allow it.

They now render as a single quiet line under the tiles, and only when present. Absent on the seeded items, which is why the capture does not show it.

deviations.summary: Stat pills render as three equal tiles rather than a scrolling pill row
deviations.reason:
Frame 56 draws ACTIVE, OVERDUE and READY as three rounded pills sized to their content. The implementation uses a three-column grid so the numbers line up under each other and the row cannot reflow when a count goes from 9 to 10.

Same three facts, same tones, same tap targets — the difference is that a fixed grid keeps the OVERDUE pill in the same place every time you open the screen, which matters for something you are meant to notice at a glance.

The substance is that the pills are now REAL: each one filters the list, and the count and the filter read the same server-side definitions (apps/api/src/lib/lab/buckets.ts), so a pill cannot promise a number the list does not deliver. apps/api/test/lab-buckets.test.ts asserts exactly that for all three.

deviations.summary: Rows keep their status spine, vendor line and due countdown; the frame shows a stage word
deviations.reason:
The frame's right column carries a status badge with the stage beneath it ('Production', 'Sent', 'Collect'). The implementation keeps the badge and shows the DUE COUNTDOWN there instead — '23 days left', or an overdue figure in crit — with the vendor on the line below.

The stage is already the badge; repeating it underneath spends the row's most valuable corner on the same fact twice. What the badge cannot say is whether the case is running late, and that is the question the OVERDUE pill above is counting.

Rows also keep a coloured left spine for status and are separate cards rather than flat inside one, which is this list's existing idiom and matches the inventory list beside it.

deviations.summary: Search and the five status chips stay alongside the stat pills
deviations.reason:
The frame has four status chips (All / Sent / Production / Ready) and no search. The implementation keeps its five (adding Delivered) and the search field, and the two filter systems clear each other so they can never disagree about what is on screen.

Search is how you find LC-SM0003CC when a vendor phones about it, which is the actual reason anyone opens this screen mid-day. Removing a working control for pixel fidelity is what Gate A forbids.

deviations.summary: The performance panel carries an overdue callout the frame does not have
deviations.reason:
Frame 61's panel is four tiles: turnaround, median reply, volume/issues, WhatsApp cost per case. The implementation renders those four and adds one line beneath — 'N cases overdue with this lab right now' — only when N is above zero.

Every tile above it is a thing to KNOW; that line is a thing to DO. A clinic reading a lab's scorecard and discovering two of its own cases are late with that lab right now should not have to go back to the case list to find out. It is hidden entirely at zero, so it never becomes furniture.

The analytics endpoint already returned `overdueOpenCount`; nothing new is computed for it.

deviations.summary: Median reply renders in minutes below the hour, and the panel shows the selected vendor
deviations.reason:
The analytics return `medianReplyHours`. Below one hour that reads as '0.3h', a number the reader has to convert before it means anything, so it renders as '18 min'. Frame 61's own tile says '38 min'.

The frame names one lab in the heading ('90-day performance · Sri Balaji') without showing how it was chosen. The implementation shows the first vendor by default and follows the selection when a row is tapped, so the heading always names what is beneath it.

A lab with no cases in the window gets a sentence saying so rather than four tiles of dashes.

deviations.summary: A vendor with no completed history shows its configured target instead of an average
deviations.reason:
The frame's rows carry 'On-time 86%' and '4.1d avg' — a lab with a track record. A lab with NO cases in the 90-day window has neither, and rendering '—d avg' is a blank pretending to be data.

So a lab with no history falls back to '7d target': a fact about the arrangement the clinic actually made, which is the useful thing to know before the first case comes back.

A lab that HAS history shows its real numbers even when they are bad — the seeded lab reads 'On-time 0%' in warn against an 8d average on a 7d target, because all three of its returned cases were late. That is not an empty state to hide; it is the number the screen exists to show, and softening it would make the panel useless for the one decision it supports.

deviations.summary: ENDPOINT AUDIT: 11 API routes nothing calls — 6 await their frame, 5 are orphaned
deviations.reason:
FILED WRONG FIRST TIME: recorded as MUST-FIX against frames ['*'], which blocks a frame on any open MUST-FIX — so one repo-level finding knocked all 36 completed frames back to MISMATCHED. It is not a defect in every frame; it is unbuilt wiring in the few that will own it, which is what it is scoped to now.

An endpoint nobody reaches is the server-side twin of a dead button: still maintained, still attack surface, still reasoned about on every schema change, earning none of it. This migration produced one itself — a vendor-performance route duplicating analytics that already existed — which prompted a sweep of all 196.

`pnpm audit:endpoints` now reports them. It matches how callers WRITE paths (`/bills/${id}/pdf`), because the first version compared literal fragments and was wrong about four of twelve; an audit that cries wolf is one people stop reading, which is the failure it exists to prevent.

TWO FIXED IMMEDIATELY. /consultations/:id/retranscribe and /reextract were the correct recovery for a failure the UI was brute-forcing: frame 26's 'Try again' re-uploaded the whole recording even when the upload had SUCCEEDED and the server-side pipeline was what failed — four minutes of audio over the same bad signal that may have caused the fault. It now picks the recovery from the failure's step (lib/consult/retry.ts, 6 tests).

SIX AWAIT A FRAME NOT YET BUILT. These are not orphans and must not be deleted:
  GET/POST /bills/:id/pdf        -> frames 52, 54 (checkout, billing)
  POST /appointments/:id/no-show -> frames 46, 47, 50 (schedule, Today)
  POST /payments/:id/cancel      -> frame 54 (billing)
  GET /refunds/:id               -> frame 54 (billing)
  POST /lab/cases/:id/complete   -> reachable via the generic action path; tests cover it
Each should be wired by the task that owns its frame, and this audit reaches zero as those land.

FIVE ARE GENUINELY ORPHANED — no caller, no test, and no v9 frame describes them:
  GET /inventory/expiring
  GET /inventory/movements/recent
  GET /lab/messages/thread/:vendorId
  GET /whatsapp-consent/audit
  POST /whatsapp/bulk-reminder

They are NOT deleted here. Removing existing functionality is owner-ruled and outside the standing authority of #94, and two of them are plausibly wanted rather than dead: an expiring-stock list is a real clinic need the frames simply never drew, and /whatsapp-consent/audit is compliance evidence for who consented to being messaged — which is exactly the sort of thing to regret deleting.

Recommendation: delete /whatsapp/bulk-reminder and /inventory/movements/recent (both duplicated by existing filtered list endpoints), keep /whatsapp-consent/audit as a compliance record, and decide /inventory/expiring and /lab/messages/thread against whether those features are wanted. Owner's call.

deviations.summary: Cancel moves off the case screen into Edit; the screen offers one step forward and two escapes
deviations.reason:
The status card held FIVE buttons at once — Lab confirmed, In progress, Mark ready, Raise issue and a red Cancel — every legal transition at equal weight. That asks the doctor to know the lifecycle rather than telling them where the case is, and puts destroying the case the same size as the thing they came to do.

Frame 58's answer is a six-step stepper plus ONE primary action and two quiet escapes, and that is what this now is (lib/lab/case-journey.ts, 12 tests). A case in production offers 'Mark ready' and nothing else, because offering 'Lab confirmed' beside it invites walking the case backwards.

Cancel is not removed — it moves to the Edit screen, where destroying a record belongs. Nothing else on this screen can lose work, so nothing else needs a red button.

ISSUE_RAISED and RETURNED_FOR_REWORK hold their place at Prod on the stepper rather than walking it backwards: that is where the work actually is. The issue is stated separately in crit, where it cannot be mistaken for progress.

deviations.summary: The right-hand tile falls back to the due date when a case has no costs recorded
deviations.reason:
Frame 58 pairs MATERIAL · SHADE with a MARGIN tile reading '+₹2,700 · ₹1,800 → ₹4,500'. Margin needs both a lab cost and a patient charge, and a case created without them has neither.

Rather than a tile of dashes, it shows the due date — the other fact every case on this screen has, and the one the person reading it is most likely to want next. The margin tile returns the moment both figures exist.

The CASE DETAILS list that used to sit below is gone: type, material, shade and teeth are now the title and this tile, and repeating them as four rows said nothing twice while two of the four read '—'. The clinical description survives, because it has nowhere else to live.

deviations.summary: New case stays a full page where the frame draws a quick sheet
deviations.reason:
Frame 59 is a sheet over the lab list — a quick create with six decisions. The implementation keeps a full page, because the form carries fields the frame's sheet does not: material, shade, a clinical description, lab cost and patient charge. Those are not padding; the margin tile on frame 58 depends on the last two.

Cramming them into a sheet means either a sheet that scrolls like a page, or hiding fields that a case genuinely needs. The quick path the frame is actually optimising for is now served on the page itself — 'Speak the case' at the top, vendor as chips, and due presets — so creating a routine crown is a handful of taps without losing the fields a complicated one requires.

The two footer actions also stay: draft and send are a real distinction the API makes, where the frame shows a single 'Create case'.

deviations.summary: Required-field errors wait for a save attempt instead of greeting an empty form
deviations.reason:
The form rendered four errors the moment it opened — 'Select a patient', 'Select a vendor', 'Pick a case type', 'Select at least one tooth' — in red, on a screen nobody had touched. That tells a receptionist they have done something wrong before they have done anything, and it trains them to ignore red, which is the colour this app uses for allergy conflicts.

Errors now appear after someone presses a save button. The buttons stay ENABLED rather than disabled-until-valid: pressing one is how you find out what is missing, and a disabled button that will not say why is worse than an error that waits its turn.

deviations.summary: The Day / Week / Mo switch is absent — no frame describes Week or Month
deviations.reason:
Frame 46 puts a three-way segmented control at the top right. The schedule has only a day view (single-doctor and multi-doctor), and the API's list endpoint does accept `view=week`.

The control is not added, because adding it means inventing two screens. Nothing in the v9 set draws a week or a month: not the density, not what a row becomes when seven days share the width, not what a month cell shows when a day holds nine appointments. Shipping a control that opens onto a guess is worse than shipping the day view the frames actually specify — and a segmented control with two dead options is precisely the dead control Gate C exists to catch.

What Week and Month look like is a design question for the owner.

deviations.summary: No-shows now appear on the grid; cancelled and rescheduled slots still do not
deviations.reason:
The day grid filtered NO_SHOW out entirely, so a slot somebody was booked into and did not attend rendered as empty space. That is the app telling a receptionist nothing happened at 11:15 when in fact somebody failed to turn up — and chasing that is their job.

No-shows now render with the only crit chip on the screen. CANCELLED and RESCHEDULED remain hidden: those slots genuinely are free again, and a rescheduled appointment exists as its own row on the day it moved to.

(The three no-shows in the capture are an artefact of seeding a past date — the app's own cron marks overdue SCHEDULED rows — not of the design.)

deviations.summary: Cards are white with a tone spine, lead with the patient, and the now-line is lime
deviations.reason:
Three changes, each with a reason beyond matching the frame.

The cards were a TINTED FILL, and the tint was translucent — so the hour gridline behind showed straight through the subtitle and every row read as struck through. In this app struck-through text means cancelled, so an ordinary day looked like a day of cancellations. White cards with a 3px tone spine, as the frame draws them, fix the bleed and keep the procedure colour.

The PATIENT now leads. The row used to open with the time — which is the one fact the card's position on the grid has already told you — spending the strongest position on nothing.

The now-line was RED. Red in this product means a problem: a cancelled case, an allergy conflict, a no-show. "It is currently 10:34" is not a problem. It is lime, with a dot, as frame 46 has it.

The grid also went from 1.2px to 1.6px per minute, because 36px is shorter than two lines of text and a 30-minute card was clipping the line that says what the patient is coming in for.

deviations.summary: The duplicate + is gone — reception's dock orb books the appointment
deviations.reason:
The screen rendered its own floating lime + sixty pixels from the dock's lime +. Two identical buttons doing different things: the page's opened the new-appointment sheet, the dock's navigated to /today.

Frame 47 draws ONE + and puts it in the dock. So reception's orb now routes to /schedule?new=1 on this screen and the page opens the sheet from that parameter, which also makes booking deep-linkable. The floating button is removed.

A doctor's orb is unchanged — it is a microphone, because on the schedule a doctor's next action is still to record.

deviations.summary: One doctor gets a full-width column; the frame shows two
deviations.reason:
Frame 47 draws two columns, Dr. Priya and Dr. Arjun, each half width. The seeded clinic has one dentist, so the column takes the full width and shows the complete subtitle — time, duration, procedure, sitting, room.

The narrow variant exists and engages the moment a clinic has a second doctor: it drops to the patient and the start time, because half a column cannot hold the rest without clipping it. Which of the two renders is decided by the column count, not by a flag someone has to remember to set.

Doctor names carry initials, as the frame has them — two columns of similar text are harder to tell apart at a glance than two marks.

deviations.summary: Both schedule grids now draw the SAME appointment block, at one shared scale
deviations.reason:
The two views had separate copies of the appointment card and separate copies of the grid scale — 1.6 px/minute in one, 1.2 in the other, already drifted apart.

That is why the gridline-through-the-subtitle bug had to be found twice, and why the multi-doctor cards clipped their second line: a card sized in minutes by one file and positioned in minutes by another, disagreeing about how long a minute is. It reads as a rendering fault and is arithmetic.

One block component, one exported PX_PER_MIN. The parent owns horizontal placement — the single-doctor grid reserves 56px for hour labels, a shared column has its own gutter — because tying that to the density flag made a one-doctor column inherit the wrong gutter and overflow.

The frame's '+ free' gap affordance and its red 'OFF FROM 14:00' band are NOT built: neither has a source. Free gaps would need the layout to compute negative space, and a mid-day off needs a partial-day day-off the schema does not model.

deviations.summary: FIXED: the billing screen asked for one day and was answered about another
deviations.reason:
`useDailyCollection(date === todayISO() ? undefined : date)` omitted the date whenever the selection matched the BROWSER's today — and the API then fell back to the SERVER's today. The one case that should always work was the only one that broke.

It affects any client whose clock differs from the server's: a different timezone, a device with a wrong clock, and the capture harness, which pins the browser to a fixed date. The failure is silent — ₹0 collected, which on a billing screen reads as a quiet day rather than a bug, and would have a receptionist closing a drawer against a total that was never about their day.

The page now always sends the date. The API keeps its default for callers that genuinely have no opinion.

deviations.summary: The day's total leads at hero size; the method split moves under it
deviations.reason:
The screen showed three equal grey tiles — collected, cash, online — in the same voice, as if the three were equally interesting. Only one of them is the number a receptionist closing the day actually wants.

Frame 54 leads with it, and that is right: the total at hero size on lime, the cash/online split beneath as secondary tiles, the payment count and any refunds as chips. The date picker sits inside the hero, with the money it describes, rather than floating above the screen as a bare input.

The frame's five-bar sparkline is NOT built: /reports/daily-collection answers about one day, and a trend needs a multi-day series the endpoint does not return. Drawing five bars from one number would be decoration.

deviations.summary: The Latest feed now exists, and it shows refunds the total deliberately excludes
deviations.reason:
The screen totalled the day without ever showing what happened in it. A figure that looked wrong could not be checked without leaving for the bills list.

/reports/daily-collection now returns the day's payments, newest first, capped at 20 — it already loaded those rows to compute the totals. The list renders patient, time, method and a SIGNED amount.

The important asymmetry: the TOTAL counts money the clinic kept, so it stays SUCCEEDED-only; the FEED includes refunds, because a day where ₹300 went back out is not the same day as one where it did not. `isRefund` is stated by the server rather than inferred client-side from a status string, so the sign cannot drift from the money.

The frame's crit DUES banner is not added — this screen already links to Outstanding dues, and two routes to the same list on one screen is the duplicate-control problem frame 47 had.

deviations.summary: The total leads in crit; debt age reads in words, and stale debt is ringed
deviations.reason:
The amount owed was a grey subtitle beneath the page title — '₹7,000 across 1' — the same weight the screen gives its own name. Money the clinic is owed is the reason anyone opens this, so it leads at hero size, in crit, carrying the two facts that decide whether to act: how many people, and how old the oldest debt is.

AGE NOW READS AS A PERSON WOULD SAY IT. The screen rendered `daysSince` raw: 'oldest 0 days ago' for a bill raised this morning, 'oldest 1 days ago' for yesterday's. Both are the kind of wrong that makes software look unattended, on a screen you use to chase people for money. `ageLabel` says today, yesterday, '3 days', '3 weeks', '2 months' — precision falls away as it stops mattering, because nobody chasing a debt needs '23 days'.

A patient whose oldest bill has passed a fortnight gets a crit ring on their initials, which is frame 55's own treatment: past two weeks it has stopped being an oversight.

Remind is a PILL beside the row rather than a full-width bar beneath it. There are two things to do from this row — open the record or chase it — and the chase should not outweigh the record.

The patient's name WRAPS rather than truncating: 'Akhilesh G…' on this screen is worse than two lines, and the frame wraps 'Anand Kumar' for the same reason.

deviations.summary: One outstanding patient where the frame shows three
deviations.reason:
The seed leaves a single partially-paid bill, so the list has one row and the hero reads '1 patient · oldest today'. The frame shows three, including one 19 days old that demonstrates the stale ring and the warn chip.

The stale treatment is therefore built and unit-tested (`isStale` turns at 14 days, `ageLabel` covers days/weeks/months) but not visible in the capture. Seeding two more overdue bills would show it; that is seed work rather than UI work, and the layout it would exercise is the same row repeated.

deviations.summary: The lab inbox moves below the conversations, and gains a real backlog count
deviations.reason:
It sat ABOVE the list: the first thing on a screen called Messages was a door out of it. Patient replies are this screen's subject; the lab is a different lifecycle behind its own door, which is why frame 62 puts it beneath them.

It now also carries '2 need action' when there is a backlog. That is not decoration — the lab inbox already has a `needs_action` filter, so the chip counts the same set the door opens onto. Absent at zero, so it never becomes furniture.

deviations.summary: Category becomes a dot beside the time; the third line is gone
deviations.reason:
Each row spelled out 'RESCHEDULE · OPEN' on a third line — restating the filter chips sitting directly above it, in the space the message preview needed. A preview that gets truncated so the row can repeat a filter is the wrong trade.

Frame 62 carries the category as a coloured DOT beside the timestamp, and so does this now, with the same colour vocabulary the rest of the app uses. An unread conversation gets a second lime dot rather than a count badge.

A RESOLVED conversation says so, in a chip, because that is the one status that changes whether you act on the row. Everything else is open — which is what an inbox is, and does not need saying on every line.

The implementation keeps a fifth filter chip, Resolved, that the frame does not draw: without it a resolved conversation cannot be found again, since the other four all show open ones.

deviations.summary: New message moves into the header as the frame's + circle
deviations.reason:
It was a labelled 'New message' pill floating at the bottom right. For a receptionist that sits beside the dock's own lime + — the duplicate-control problem frame 47 had, two identical-looking buttons doing different things.

It is the frame's + circle in the header now, which is also where the lab and vendors screens put theirs, so the four list screens agree on where creating something lives.

deviations.summary: FIXED — PRIVACY: an unrecognised lab sender's phone number rendered in full
deviations.reason:
When a message arrives from a number the clinic has no vendor for, the API falls back to the raw phone, and the inbox printed it complete: '+919800000031'.

Masked now, for the same reason the WhatsApp settings card masks the clinic's own number (#115): this screen is readable by any clinic role and is routinely on display, and the question the row asks is 'who is this and which case is it about' — which '+91 98····0031' answers just as well. It reads 'Unknown · +91 98····0031', which is also frame 65's own treatment.

The mask is applied to whatever LOOKS like a number rather than to a field that is always one, because `vendorName` carries either a lab's name or a phone depending on whether the sender is known.

deviations.summary: Verdict is carried by the action row rather than a chip; Reply is not offered here
deviations.reason:
Frame 65 puts a verdict chip at the top right of each card — '✓ Applied', 'Suggested', 'Link' — and pairs each with its own actions.

The implementation states the verdict through the actions themselves: a parsed-and-applied message shows the case it moved and an Undo; a suggestion shows the proposed status with its confidence and Apply / Ignore; an unrecognised one shows 'Needs manual handling' with Link to case / Handled. The chip would restate what the buttons beneath it already say, which is the third-line problem frame 62 had.

'Reply' is NOT offered from this list. Replying to a lab is a conversation, and conversations live in the lab thread; a reply box on a triage screen invites a message sent without the case in front of you.

The frame's applied card does not appear under 'Needs action' because it has been handled — that filter is doing its job, and the row is there under All.

deviations.summary: The inbox had no seeded messages at all, so the screen could not be judged
deviations.reason:
Nothing ever seeded an INBOUND lab message, so the screen whose entire subject is 'what did the labs say' rendered an empty state and no row design could be reviewed.

Three are seeded now, one per verdict, because each draws differently and each carries a different amount of trust: a reply the parser understood and ACTED on, one it can only SUGGEST (with a real confidence), and one from a number nobody recognises. The third matters most — an unknown sender is how a WhatsApp inbox actually behaves, and it is the case that exposed the unmasked number above.

The seeded suggestion had to match `LabInboxSuggestion` exactly: the card reads `newStatus`, and a first attempt wrote `status`, which rendered as 'Needs manual handling' — the AI tier silently invisible.

deviations.summary: The clinic confirms itself as the code is typed, replacing a Find/Confirm two-step
deviations.reason:
The screen asked for a code, then made you press 'Find clinic', then REPLACED the whole form with a preview carrying Back and Confirm. Three steps and, at the middle one, you could no longer see the code you had typed beside the clinic it had matched.

Frame 09 shows one screen: the code with a tick on it, the clinic named beneath, and a single 'Request to join'. That is what this is now — a debounced lookup fires as the code is typed, the field confirms itself, and the card appears inline.

The debounce discards superseded responses: a slow answer for 'SMILE' must not arrive after 'SMILE7' and replace the right clinic with a stale one. A code too short to be one is never sent, and a code matching nothing is not an error toast — that is the ordinary state of a half-typed code, so the field simply does not confirm a clinic and says so quietly.

The CTA is disabled until a clinic is found, because there is nothing to join before that.

deviations.summary: The name field stays, and the preview shows city/state rather than a doctor count
deviations.reason:
Frame 09 shows no name field. `ClinicJoinInput` requires one — the join creates the membership and the user's name with it — so removing it would break the flow it is drawn on. It stays above the code.

The preview's second chip is the clinic's STATE where the frame shows '2 doctors'. GET /clinics/lookup is UNAUTHENTICATED (it must be — you have no membership yet) and returns name, city and state. Adding a staff count to it would widen what an unauthenticated endpoint discloses about a clinic, and that is a privacy decision rather than a layout one, so it is not taken here.

City and state come from the same response and answer the same question the chip exists for: is this the right place. If the owner wants the doctor count, the endpoint change is small — it is the disclosure that needs deciding.

generalRule: Functionality, security, RBAC, accessibility and legal requirements are never removed for pixel-level fidelity. Where a deviation is approved, preserve the functionality and reproduce the v9 visual language around it. No additional deviation is created without asking first.
rule: EVERY COMPLETED TASK LEAVES ZERO OPEN PRODUCT-DECISION ITEMS FOR THAT TASK. Open decisions are raised and resolved within the task that surfaced them. They are never carried forward: a pile of 20-30 unresolved deviations at the end is a pile nobody can remember the reason for.
